extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent litigators, and law students studying patent specification and claim construction
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for preparing a patent specification and for construing patents (including the role of drawings, claims, enablement, and the courts/juries). Covers also related license-scope/forfeiture principles. Aimed at guiding how to write, interpret, and litigate specifications and claims under U.S. practice (historical statutes/cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory written-description and disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Before receiving a patent the inventor must deliver a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making, constructing, using, and compounding the same 'in such full, clear, and exact terms, avoiding unnecessary prolixity, as to enable any person skilled in the art... to make, construct, compound, and use the same'; for machines the principle and several modes of application must be explained; the specification must particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination claimed; and where the nature of the case admits, drawings or specimens and models must be filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core statutory mandate (Act of July 4, 1836, §6, re‑enacted 1870). The text insists on sufficiency of description and drawings/models where applicable. The preparation must enable a skilled artisan to practice the invention; the claim must point out what is claimed as new. Failure to satisfy these statutory requirements can invalidate the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification is part of the patent and controls its construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Under U.S. law the specification (and drawings annexed) are filed before the patent and are referred to in the patent; the specification forms part of the letters-patent and may control the generality of the patent's terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with earlier English practice. Drawings annexed in compliance with statute are part of the specification and are to be regarded in construction. Where the patent language is ambiguous, the specification may limit or explain it; but it cannot supply an invention not described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court role in claim construction; jury role for factual matters
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the province of the court to determine what is intended to be patented and whether the invention is described with reasonable certainty (questions of law). Where terms of art or surrounding circumstances require factual determination, those matters go to the jury, which takes the court's conditional construction and applies it to found facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where no technical terms or factual background are in dispute, construction is for the court. If expert evidence is needed to explain terms of art or surrounding circumstances, the jury resolves those facts and thereby conditions the ultimate construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement (specification must enable a skilled person to practise the invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe the invention in such full, clear, and exact terms that a skilful person in the art can put it into practice from the specification itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is typically a question of fact for the jury on expert evidence: experts must testify there is enough on the face of the specification to enable production or reproduction without difficulty. Ambiguities that prevent an artisan from making/using the invention render the specification insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification may limit patent generality but repugnancy voids patent
rubrics_metrics.description: While a specification may control and restrict the generality of the patent terms, if there is a clear repugnancy between the description in the specification and the invention stated in the letters-patent, the patent will be void because the statute is not complied with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule allowing the specification to control patent wording cannot save a patent where the patent claims an invention not described in the specification. Cases cited show patents void where the title/patent covered something the specification did not describe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberal construction of patents (ut res magis valeat quam pereat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are to be construed liberally and not with over-nice or strict rules; the object is to ascertain, from the fair sense of the words, the nature and extent of the inventor's claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American courts favor a fair and liberal view in light of the constitutional purpose to promote science and useful arts. Formal or inartificial expression should not defeat a clearly ascertainable claim. Nevertheless statutory requisites must be met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must distinguish between old and new (point out what is claimed)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the patentee uses prior (old) matter, the specification must distinguish what is old from what is new and must point out in what the invention or improvement consists; failing to do so may render the patent void or broader than the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a specification mixes old and new without clearly ascertaining what part is claimed as new, the patent may be void because it either covers too much (includes old matter) or is ambiguous as to what is claimed. Courts will not carve away portions to save an overbroad claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims' purpose: to ascertain the extent of the new invention (not a how-to)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is introduced to ascertain and declare the extent of what the patentee claims as new; it is not intended as a description of the means to perform the invention or as an aid to the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims identify the boundaries of the monopoly; they are not a substitute for the descriptive disclosure required to enable practice. The claim may, however, be construed in light of the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable certainty requirement (avoidance of vagueness)
rubrics_metrics.description: It must appear with reasonable certainty what the patentee intends to claim; inaccuracy or imperfect wording will not vitiate the specification if, by fair interpretation of the whole, the nature and extent of the claim are clear; but if wholly ambiguous and uncertain the patent is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases should not be read in isolation; the entire specification and drawings should be taken together. Courts will uphold imperfect language where a reasonable construction identifies the invention, but will void patents that leave courts guessing or relying on conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings constitute part of the specification and can explain it
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings annexed to a specification (where admissible) form part of the specification and are to be regarded in construction; drawings not expressly referred to may still be used to explain the specification provided they accompany it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare words and drawings: if together they enable a skilled mechanic to perform the invention, the specification is sufficient. Drawings can clarify ambiguous textual descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives of the specification: public enablement and public notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification has two objects: (1) to make known the manner of constructing/using the invention so artisans can make and use it after patent expiration; (2) to put the public in possession of what the patentee claims as his own invention so the public can determine whether it is already known and to guard against prejudice or innocent infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These twin objectives underlie the disclosure and claim rules: disclosure for enablement, and clear claims/description for public notice and to prevent overreaching by the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparing specifications for novelty: sufficiency and identity questions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a defendant attacks novelty by producing a prior patent/specification, two questions arise: (a) whether the court alone can decide from mere comparison that the two inventions are identical; (b) whether the prior specification must itself be so clear and complete as to sustain a patent, or whether a mere hint may be enough to defeat a subsequent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This raises evidentiary and legal issues; the text refers to detailed English discussions and to the chapter on actions at law. The sufficiency of a prior disclosure to anticipate is a substantive question to be examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inaccuracy not fatal if fair interpretation reveals the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: While the specification must be reasonably certain, it is not necessary that the language be technical; inaccuracy or inartful expression will not vitiate the specification if the court can, by fair interpretation of the whole, ascertain clearly what is claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will construe drawings and text together and favor a reasonable interpretive approach rather than striking down patents on small drafting imperfections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee estoppel by admissions in a license (unless deceived/misled)
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee who has taken a license is estopped by any admissions contained in it as to the patent's validity, unless he can avoid their effect by showing he was deceived and misled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a licensee accepts a license and later repudiates it to assert invalidity, admissions in the license may bar him from contesting validity absent proof of deception. Practical effect: drafting and negotiation of licenses can create assertions binding the licensee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture clause in license gives patentee 'double remedy'
rubrics_metrics.description: A clause making a license void on non-payment (or breach) is regarded as giving the patentee a double remedy: he may either enforce collection of what is due or treat the license as forfeited and proceed to enjoin the licensee as an infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law treats such clauses as allowing election of remedies. Practical implication: license drafting and enforcement strategy must consider remedies and whether to sue for breach or for infringement after declaring forfeiture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breach of license condition (territory/purpose) may work forfeiture and support injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: A breach of a condition in a license (e.g., selling manufactured products out of licensed territory, or using the licensed material for prohibited purposes) works a forfeiture and the licensee may be enjoined as an infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: territorial use limits, restrictions on sale/use for particular purposes. Courts have enforced territorial and purpose limits where the license clearly imposed them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of license tied to authorized establishment/territory/purpose at grant time
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to use an invention 'at his own establishment, but not to be disposed of to others' authorizes only use at that establishment and does not permit authorizing others or using it at another establishment; similarly, a license to a railroad extended no further than the road in use or authorized to be constructed at the time of granting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: License scope is interpreted against expansion by later corporate changes or consolidations; specific wording limiting location or purpose will be enforced literally. Drafters should be precise about permitted uses, locations, and successors/assigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: When patentee treats license as forfeited defendant may rely on prior rights (with limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee elects to treat a license as forfeited for breach and proceeds against the licensee as an unlicensed user, the defendant may be remitted to rights he had before the license (e.g., a prior title under a former patent term) and may set up those rights in defense; but whether this permits avoiding admissions in the license about validity is questionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The doctrine allows a defendant to assert antecedent rights that survived into the licensed term when the patentee elects forfeiture; courts differ/limit how far this undoes admissions in the license itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction in light of specification when claim immediately follows description
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the claim immediately follows the description it may be construed in connection with the explanations contained in the specification and be restricted accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are read in context; placement and proximity to descriptive matter affects how broadly claims will be interpreted. This supports limiting a claim by the specification where appropriate.
